title: The Customer Success Playbook for Solo Founders
summary: A practical framework for solo founders to prevent churn using five simple health signals (core feature activation, usage breadth, support sentiment, champion engagement, billing health) that can be monitored in 15 minutes weekly. The system uses scoring bands to trigger specific interventions, from proactive outreach for at-risk customers to 48-hour escalation for critical cases.
content:
I ran customer success at a 200-person SaaS company before going independent. We had a dedicated CS team, a six-figure Gainsight contract, health scores updated daily by data pipelines, and quarterly QBRs for every account over $50K ARR. It was impressive. It was also overkill — most of what actually prevents churn can be done by a single founder with a spreadsheet.
When I started advising solo founders on retention, I noticed a pattern. The founders who worried most about churn were the ones doing the least about it. They'd look at their monthly churn number, feel sick, and then go back to building features. No outreach. No intervention. No system.
Here's the playbook I've built and tested across seven solo-founded SaaS products.
Gainsight's framework uses dozens of signals fed into a weighted scoring model. That's the right approach at scale. For a solo founder managing 30-150 customers, you need five signals you can check in 15 minutes a week. Here's what I use:
Signal 1: Core Feature Activation (Weight: 30%)
Signal 2: Usage Breadth (Weight: 20%)
Signal 3: Support Sentiment Trend (Weight: 15%)
Signal 4: Champion Engagement (Weight: 20%)
Signal 5: Billing Health (Weight: 15%)
Each signal gets scored 0-2 (0 = red, 1 = yellow, 2 = green). Total score ranges from 0-10. I use three bands:
8-10: Healthy — Focus on expansion
5-7: At Risk — Proactive outreach this week
0-4: Critical — Intervention within 48 hours
The health score is useless if it doesn't trigger action. Here are the specific triggers I set up for every founder I advise:
Usage Drop Trigger: Core feature usage drops by 40%+ week-over-week. Send a check-in email within 48 hours. Not "we noticed you haven't been using [feature]" — that's creepy. Instead: "I was reviewing how teams like yours are using [feature] and put together a quick walkthrough of three workflows that [similar company] uses. Want me to send it over?"
Feature Adoption Trigger: Customer has been active for 30+ days but hasn't used a feature

title: I Wrote Integration Tests for My MCP Failure Library. Here's the Pattern That Caught 3 Hidden Bugs.
summary: An exploration of why unit tests alone failed to catch production bugs in an MCP failure library, and how a real integration test harness revealed hidden issues with component interactions. The author demonstrates that testing real STDIO transport, actual databases, and production retry logic surfaces failures that mocks cannot.
content:
I'd been shipping fixes to my MCP failure library for weeks. Every release felt solid. Then I've written one real integration test - and three "fixed" bugs weren't fixed at all.
My failure library is an MCP server that stores crash patterns so AI agents can warn each other before hitting the same bug twice. Think of it as shared memory for tool errors: agent A hits a timeout talking to an external API, records the failure pattern, and agent B checks the library before making the same call. It works - when the server is running and the database is primed.
But getting it to work reliably in production was a different story. I'd been testing each component in isolation: the SQLite layer with unit tests, the MCP transport with mock clients, the retry logic with controlled timeouts. Each passed with flying colors. I had 90%+ coverage.
And yet, in production, things broke every other day. A fix that worked locally would fail in CI. A feature that passed every unit test would crash the first time two agents used it simultaneously.
The issue wasn't the code - it was the Interactions. A tool call that succeeded in isolation could fail when the session tracking layer hadn't initialized. A fix that worked with one MCP client crashed with another. Unit tests proved individual functions were mathematically correct, but they couldn't prove the system worked as a whole.
I wrote a short integration test harness that spins up the real MCP server, connects a real client, and runs end-to-end scenarios. No mocks, no stubs, no fakes - the actual STDIO transport, the real SQLite database, the production retry logic.

title: How MTProto Obfuscation and FakeTLS Defeat Deep Packet Inspection
summary: A technical breakdown of how Telegram's MTProto protocol uses obfuscation layers to evade state-level deep packet inspection, including XOR obfuscation, random padding, and FakeTLS techniques. The approach defeats simple signature-based filtering by randomizing initial bytes and packet distributions that would otherwise be identifiable to DPI systems.
content:
Deep Packet Inspection (DPI) blocks Telegram by recognising the unique byte signatures of its transport protocol. Standard MTProto uses a fixed 0xEE prefix on the first packet and specific handshake patterns – easy for state-level filters like Russia's TSPU or Iran's DPI to match and drop. MTProto proxies exist to bypass these filters, and they do it with three layers: obfuscation, random padding, and FakeTLS. Here’s how each works and why DPI can’t keep up.
Telegram's transport layer is not vanilla TLS. It uses a custom framing protocol over TCP with its own built-in encryption. The first four bytes of a connection are either:
0xEEEEEEEE for plain (deprecated)
0xEFEFEFEF for abridged (no checksum)
Or an intermediate mode with 0xEE prefix
These magic bytes are DPI candy. Filter operators can write a single rule: drop any TCP connection with first byte = 0xEE. That's why raw MTProto connections are blocked in most censored regions.
The simplest evasion wraps the MTProto connection in a thin XOR obfuscation layer. The client sends a random 64-byte "obfuscation envelope" before the actual MTProto handshake. The proxy decrypts it and forwards the inner traffic normally.
The envelope structure:
[client_random (64 bytes)] [encrypted_mtproto_data...]

The first byte of client_random is 0xEF to look like abridged mode to the proxy, but the rest are random. The proxy sends back its own 64-byte random response. After this exchange, both sides derive an XOR key from the random data to obfuscate subsequent packets.
This defeats simple signature-based DPI because the first byte on the wire is no longer a known magic value. However, traffic analysis can still detect the pattern of a 64-byte initial exchange followed by consistent packet sizes – which leads to the next layer.

title: Solon AOT & Native: Three Phases to a GraalVM Native Executable
summary: A guide to Solon's three-phase native compilation pipeline that simplifies GraalVM configuration through automatic AOT processing. Phase 2 handles proxy pre-compilation, class indexing, and metadata generation, with support for any JDK (not just GraalVM), making the build more approachable than typical Java native compilation.
content:
When you hear "Java native compilation with GraalVM," you probably think of configuration hell — endless JSON metadata files, trial-and-error reflection registrations, and build scripts that take more effort than the application itself.
Solon takes a different path. Its AOT pipeline compiles in three phases, where each phase feeds into the next. The framework's "restraint" philosophy — minimal dynamic proxies, explicit configuration over magic — makes native compilation more straightforward than you'd expect.
Let me walk through how it works, what you get, and where you might need to reach for the manual override.
Solon Native compilation is three distinct stages, each independently runnable:



Phase
What it does
Maven command
JDK




1
Standard Java compilation
mvn clean -DskipTests=true package
jdk8+


2
Solon AOT processing
mvn clean -DskipTests=true -P aot package
jdk8+ (any JDK)


3
GraalVM native-image
mvn clean -DskipTests=true -P native native:compile
graalvm jdk17+



Phase 2 is where Solon does the heavy lifting.
The Solon AOT processor (SolonAotProcessor from the solon-aot module) runs automatically after mvn package when you use the -P aot profile. What does it do?
It bootstraps your application at compile time, runs through the natural startup flow, and captures everything the framework needs to work without runtime reflection:
Proxy class pre-compilation — Dynamic AOP proxies that would normally be generated via ASM bytecode at runtime are compiled to real .class files at build time
Class index generation — If your project has many classes, this index accelerates startup by avoiding classpath scanning
GraalVM metadata generation — Reflection, resource, and serialization metadata are written in GraalVM's native configuration format automatically

My First SIEM Deployment: Logs, Lessons, and a Little Bit of Chaos

Setting the Stage: My CloudShare Playground & Modifications

title: How I Built a Free Audible Credit Value Optimizer — and Why Most Subscribers Waste Their Credits
summary: A tool and methodology for optimizing Audible credit usage by calculating a value score based on duration, rating, and retail price. The formula reveals that credit decisions can differ by $40+ in value, showing how subscribers can make data-driven choices rather than accepting the default purchase prompt.
content:
I've been an Audible subscriber for years. Every month I get my one credit, and every month I face the same question:
Is this book worth my credit?
The answer is almost never obvious. A 5-hour novella costs the same as a 45-hour epic fantasy. A $12 self-help book costs the same credit as a $38 blockbuster. And yet, most people — myself included — just pick a book and click "Buy with 1 Credit" without thinking about the numbers.
So I built a tool to fix that.
Here's the simple math:
One Audible credit costs $14.95 (on the standard Premium Plus plan). That credit can buy you:
A 5-hour book at $12.99 → you lose $1.96 by using a credit
A 45-hour epic at $38.99 → you save $24.04 by using a credit
A 60-hour classic at $19.99 → you save $5.04, but your cost per hour is just $0.33



The difference between the best and worst uses of a credit can be $40+ in lost value. Multiply that by 12 months and you're talking about real money.
But here's the thing: Audible doesn't tell you this. Their interface shows you a price and a "Buy with 1 Credit" button, but no context on whether that's actually a good deal.
I wanted to solve this problem with data. The idea was simple: create a formula that factors in everything that makes a credit decision smart.
After some iteration, I landed on this:
Value Score = (Duration in hours × Star Rating) / Price in USD

Why this formula?
Duration rewards long books — a 40-hour book is objectively better value than a 5-hour one for the same credit
Rating rewards quality — a 4.8-star book is worth more than a 3.5-star one, even at the same length
Price accounts for retail value — if a book costs $38, using a credit saves you real money. If it costs $12, you're better off buying directly
The result is a single number. Here's how to interpret it:



Value Score
Verdict




8.0+
Excellent credit value. Use a credit.


5.0 - 7.9
Good value. Worth a credit if you want the book.


3.0 - 4.9
Marginal. Consider buying directly.


Below 3.0
Poor credit value.

title: How Vision-Language Models Learned to Reason About Space (10 Papers, One Thread)
summary: A 10-chapter research survey tracing how vision-language models evolved from describing images without spatial understanding to reasoning about 3D geometry and metric distances. The papers chronicle successive solutions to representational mismatches between discrete language tokens and continuous 3D geometry, from synthetic data augmentation to depth APIs.
content:
This is a cross-post. The original (with diagrams, code, and cheat sheets for every chapter) lives on my blog:
The Evolution of Spatial VLMs
Vision-language models can describe a warehouse photo in fluent prose — and then fail to answer "how many meters is the forklift from the shelf?" They see but don't perceive. Over 2024–2026 a line of research closed that gap step by step, and the arc is remarkably coherent once you read it through a single lens:
The representational mismatch between discrete language tokens and continuous 3D geometry — and the successive attempts to close it.
I wrote a 10-chapter course tracing that arc paper by paper. Here's the map, with a one-line "why this paper had to exist" for each. Full chapter (analogies + mermaid diagrams + runnable code) is linked on each.
BLINK: See but Not Perceive — The diagnosis. Humans 95.7% vs GPT-4V 51.3% on tasks people solve "in the blink of an eye." VLMs read images as a bag of semantic concepts, not geometry.


SpatialVLM: Data Is the Answer — Reframe spatial blindness as a data problem, not an architecture one. Lift 2D web images to metric 3D and synthesize 2B spatial VQA pairs.


SpatialRGPT — Point at a Region, Plant the Depth — Add region grounding + a gracefully-degrading depth plugin. The first VLM to point at "this object" and reason in metric 3D.


SpatialBot — Learning to Read Depth — Make depth queryable: a Depth API the model can call instead of guessing.


Thinking in Space — From single images to video: does the model build a cognitive map and remember space?


OmniSpatial — Draw the map of the ability itself: a comprehensive taxonomy of spatial reasoning.


Perspective-Aware Reasoning (APC) — "If I stood over there…" — mental imagery to break egocentric bias.


Depth-native VLMs — DepthVLM vs DepthLM — What if the VLM is the depth sensor? Two takes on baking depth in natively.


Verifiable RL for Spatial Reasoning — Spatial skill isn't only more labels; a verifiable reward can activate latent

def rel_lum(h: str) -> float:
    def f(c: float) -> float:
        return c / 12.92 if c <= 0.04045 else ((c + 0.055) / 1.055) ** 2.4
    r, g, b = (f(c) for c in hex_to_rgb(h))
    return 0.2126 * r + 0.7152 * g + 0.0722 * b

def contrast(a: str, b: str) -> float:
    la, lb = rel_lum(a), rel_lum(b)
    hi, lo = max(la, lb), min(la, lb)
    return (hi + 0.05) / (lo + 0.05)
